Being aggrieved by the said discrimination, the petitioner field an application on 20-7-2006 before the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh with the prayer for refixation of the pay scale of the petitioner Jamadar as like as Driver of the Supreme Court through the Registrar of the Supreme Court. Thereafter, the matter was placed before the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh for his opinion so that the file may be placed before the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs for enhancement of pay scale of the petitioner as like as the pay scale of the Driver of the Supreme Court the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh on 28-2-2007 opined with the comment "yes" thereby approved the same and thus directed the concerned authority to implement the same. 

 11. He further submits that the recommendation as made by the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh (Annexure-G to the writ petition) was in the following manner: 

 12. He further submits that under the provisions of Article 113 of the Constitution the Hon'ble Chief Justice has the constitutional authority to determine the terms and conditions of the service of the employees of the Supreme Court including their appointment. In pursuant to the said constitutional power the Hon'ble Chief Justice decided to upgrade the pay scale of the petitioner and other Jamadars to the pay scale of Driver who are getting the scale of Taka 3000-5920 i.e. in Grade-XVI under the National Pay Scale of 2005. The Hon'ble Chief Justice has also decided to pay them VIP allowances as they are entitled to. He further submits that the impugned memo under Annexure-'L and L(1)' of the writ petition have been issued by the Deputy Secretary who has turned down the decision of the Hon'ble Chief Justice taken by him in pursuant to the power and authority vested upon him under Article 113 of the Constitution. He further submits that the provisions of Article 113 of the Constitution other than the Recruitment Rules of 1987, no Rules have been framed determining in the terms and conditions of the Services of the officers and employees of the Supreme Court, the recommendation of the Hon'ble Chief Justice is a decision of the Supreme Court, which is final and binding upon all the authorities serving under the Republic according to Article 112 of the Constitution. He further submits that earlier similar dispute was raised in the case of drivers for whom the Hon'ble Chief Justice has taken a decision to allow them over time allowances for 250 hours per months at the rate of 2,670 22 + 8 x 250 totaling Taka 3,792.50 per month. The calculation was made on the basis of taking into consideration of the basis pay of a Driver. 

 "Upon reading this article we find that the learned Chief Justice is authorized to determine the conditions of the service of the staff of the Supreme Court subject to the provisions of any Act of the Parliament. Thereafter, in the absence of any Act contrary thereto we find no difficulty in holding that the decision of the learned Chief Justice shall prevail over the decision of the Ministry of Finance with regard to the condition in question of the service of the staff of the Supreme Court and therefore the impugned memo is found to be without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect." 

 15. The above decision is a declared law of this land which is also final and binding upon all the authorities. He further submits that the present case of the Jamadars are also same and covered by the said decision of the Supreme Court and, as such, the petitioner as well as the other Jamadars of the Supreme Court are entitled to get the benefit of the judgment of the Supreme Court in the same manner as it has been allowed in the case of Drivers of the Supreme Court. He further submits that the power and authority of the Hon'ble Chief Justice as contemplated under Article 146 of the Indian Constitution, as like as Article 113 of our Constitution. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Supreme Court Employees Welfare Association vs Union of India reported in AIR 1990 (SC) 334 and also reported in 1989 SCC (L&S) 569 Specifically paragraph 56 and 57 of the said decision. 

 16. Mr Md Salahuddin Dolon, the learned Advocate for the petitioner further submits that, under Article 113 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, it is the Chief Justice who is the Supreme authority to take decision with regard to terms and conditions of the service of the officers and employees of the Supreme Court and there is no scope on the part of the executive to change, alter or turn down any decision of the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh. He further submits that in case of any disagreement with the decision of the Hon'ble Chief Justice with regard to the terms and conditions of service of the officers and employees of the Supreme Court, the President or the government may exchange thoughts and views but not a Deputy Secretary is empowered to turn down a decision of the Hon'ble Chief Justice. He further submits that to protect the Supreme Court from the arbitrary and illegal action of the executive, the Hon'ble Chief Justice has to frame rules with the assistance of his own Justices and Officers of the Supreme Court. He further submits that due to distinguish function, allocation, status of staff and officers of the Supreme Court, the Constitution has created there as separate entity apart from the other services. He further submits that the job of the Officers and Staffs of the Supreme Court are highly technical and high mental standing. For which the Hon'ble Chief Justice has been vested with a Constitutional power to make rules for the Officer and Employee of the Supreme Court. He further submits that Officers and Employees of the Supreme Court who get a special pay structure because of their Supremacy in the work-field, work load, skilled responsibility undertaken by the employees and duties of various categories. He further submits that the summary as has been placed before the Ministry by the Registrar of the Supreme' Court who has acted as an agent of the Hon'ble Chief Justice and the summary sent by him should be dealt to have been sent by the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh. He further submits that the claim of the petitioner to refix the salary by enhancing the salary with the salary of the drivers are legal and both the job of the Drivers and the Jamaders are similar and they have work load with the Justices of the Supreme Court and their claim is very legitimate. He further submits that if the petitioner and Jamaders had not been promoted as Jamader, they would have been more higher scale than the Drivers because of their scale; MLSS starts from 2850 and during the last 15-20 years all the Jamaders would have entitlement of 15-20 increments, which would have been increased the pay too much higher level than they are claiming now. 

 17. Mr Karuna Moy Chakma the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing with Mr Eunus Ali, Mr Titas Hillol Rema and Mr Nazibur Rahman, the learned Assistant Attorney Generals for the respondents submits that the petitioner and other Jamadars having been working with the Justices for whole time from 8 -OOAM to 9-00 PM they are obviously entitled to get VIP allowance and over time, as it has been decided in Writ Petition No.3599 of 2000. He further submits that under Rule 42 of the Bangladesh Service Rules, Part No.1, the pay (Scale) drawing by the petitioners cannot be reduced and they are also entitled to get protection of their pay. He further submits that even though the Drivers and Jamadars are working in the same grade and their service with the Justices is similar but their scales are different and since the Jamadars are working under the different scale then that of Driver they are not entitled to get the scale of Driver of the Justice of the Supreme Court. He further submits that the doctrine of equal work and equal pay does not apply as their job is not similar. But during his argument, he found it difficult to argue regarding turn down of the reference of the Hon'ble Chief Justice of the Supreme Court by the Deputy Secretary of the Ministry of Finance. But he submits that before turn down of the reference of the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, the President of the People's Republic or the government ought to have exchange thought and views between themselves as the summary was sent by the Supreme Court was placed before different Ministries including the Ministry of Law Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, Ministry of Establishment and lastly Ministry of Finance. 

 23. The matter was placed before the Chief Justice of Bangladesh on 28-2-2007 by the Registrar of the Supreme Court and he has consented to the proposal. The said proposal reads as follows: 

 24. After the consent and endorsement of the Chief Justice the matter was sent to the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs. In reply to the same, the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs vide Memo No. বিচার-২/১ ই-১/২০০৭-২০১৭ dated 16-5-2007 requested the Registrar of Bangladesh Supreme Court to supply detailed summary for the information to the Ministry, which runs thus: 

 113.(।) Appointments to the staff of the Supreme Court shall be made by the Chief Justice, or such other judge or officer of that Court as he may direct, and shall be made in accordance with Rules made with the previous approval of the President by the Supreme Court. (2) Subject to the provisions of any Act of Parliament the conditions of service of members of the staff of the Supreme Court shall be such as may be prescribed by Rules made by that Court. Upon reading the above quoted article we find that the Hon'ble Chief Justice is authorized to determine the conditions of the service of the staffs of the Supreme Court subject to the provision of any act of the Parliament. Therefore, in the absence of any Act contrary thereto, we find to difficulty in holding that the decision of the learned Chief Justice shall prevail over the decision of the Ministry of Finance with regard to the conditions in question of the service of the staff of the Supreme Court and therefore, the impugned memo is found to be without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect." 

 30. In the said case also the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh referred the matter to the Ministry vide Memo No. 504 dated 20-1-2000 for awarding over time to the Drivers of the Supreme Court, which has been turned down by the Ministry of Finance dated 7-6-2000 and the said refusal has been challenged in Writ Petition No.3599 of 2000. The judgment and order of the said writ petition has not been interfered by the Supreme Court and now the Drivers of the Supreme Court are getting the benefit of over time. 

 31. In the present case also the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh referred the matter to the Ministry of Finance as he is authorized to do under Article 113 of the Constitution. 

 32. It appears that under Article 112 of the Constitution all Authorities, Executive and Judicial in the Republic shall act in aid of the Supreme Court and under Part 6 of the Constitution the Chief Justice is the Head of the Judicially, an organ amongst three of the State. Under Article 113, the appointment of the Staff of the Supreme Court shall be governed by the Chief Justice and conditions of service of the Staff and Employees of the Supreme Court shall be governed by the Supreme Court prescribed by the Rules, subject to the provisions of any Act of Parliament. In the instant case Parliament has not yet promulgated any Act, Rules and Regulations or the Constitutions of the Service of the members and staffs of the Supreme Court. Nor the Supreme Court has yet formed any Rules for the terms and conditions of service of the Staff of the Supreme Court (terms and conditions of service has not been made by the Supreme Court). Since no Rules has yet been made by the Supreme Court, the recommendation made by the Chief Justice is binding upon the executive authorities according to Article 112 of the Constitution which has also been held in the case of Md Hanif Ullah vs Secretary, Ministry of Finance, Bangladesh passed in Writ Petition No. 3599 of 2000. 

 "Under Article 146(2), the Constitutions of the Service of Officers and Servants of the Supreme Court shall be such as may be prescribed by the Rules made by the Chief Justice of India or by some other judge or officer of the Court authorized by the Chief Justice of India to make Rules for the purpose. This is however subject to the provisions of any law that may be made by Parliament. It is apparent from Article 146(2) that it is primarily the responsibility of the Parliament to lay down the conditions of service of the officers and servants of the Supreme Court but so long as Parliament does not lay down such conditions of service, the Chief Justice of India or some other judge or officer of the Court authorized by the Chief Justice of India is empowered to make rules for the purpose. The legislative function of Parliament has been delegated to the Chief Justice of India by Article 146(2). It is not disputed that the function of the Chief Justice of India or The judge or the officer of the Court authorized by him in framing rules laying down the conditions of service is legislative in nature the conditions of service that may be prescribed by the Rules framed by the Chief justice of India under Article 146(2) will also necessarily include salary, allowances, leave and pensions of the officers and servants of the Supreme Court. The provision to Article 146(2) puts a restriction on the power of the Chief Justice of India by providing that the rules made under Article 146(2) shall, so far as pensions, require the approval of the President of India. Prima facie, therefore the conditions of service of the employees of the Supreme Court that are laid down by the Chief Justice of India by framing the rules will be final and conclusive, except that with regard to salaries, allowances, leave or pensions the approval of the President of India is required. In other words if the President of India does not approve of the salaries allowances, leave or pensions it will not have any effect. The reason for requiring the approval of the President or the Government of India regarding salaries, allowances leave or pensions is the involvement of the financial liability of the Government. One important thing that is to be noticed is that under clause (3) of Article ।46 the administrative expenses of the Supreme Court including all salaries allowances, leave and pensions payable to or in respect of the officers and servants of the Court shall be charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India. In view of the provision of clause (3), such administrative expenses shall not be submitted to the vote of Parliament, as provided in Article 113 of the Constitution. It is apparent that in order to maintain the independence of the judiciary, the framers of the Constitution thought it wise and expedient to make such a provision as contained in clause (3) of Article 146." 

 "The real question is how and in what manner the President of India should act after the Chief Justice of India submits to him the Rules framed by him relating to the salaries, allowances, leave and pensions of the officers and servants of the Supreme Court. The President of India is the highest dignitary of the State and the Chief Justice of India also is a high dignitary of the State. Upon a comparative study of some other similar provisions of the Constitution, we find that under Article 98(3), the President of India has been empowered to make rules regulating the recruitments and the conditions of service of persons appointed to the secretarial staff of the House of the People or the Council of States, after consultation with the Speaker or the House of the People or the Chairman of the Council of States, as the case may be. Article 148(5) provides that the conditions of service of persons serving in the Indian Audit and Accounts Department and the administrative powers of the Comptroller and Auditor-General shall be such as may be prescribed by rules made by the President of India after consultation with the Comptroller and Auditor-General. Similarly, the Governor has been empowered under Article 187(3) to make rules regulating the recruitment, and the conditions of service of persons appointed to the secretarial staff of the Assembly or the Council after consultation with the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly or the Chairman of the Legislative Council, as the cause may be, thus it appears that except in the cases of the officers and servants of the Supreme Court and those of the High Courts in other cases either the President of India or the Governor has been empowered to frame rules. 

 So far as the Supreme Court and the High Courts are concerned, the Chief Justice of India and the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court are empowered to frame rules subject to this that when the Rules are framed by the Chief Justice of India or by the Chief Justice of the High Court relating to salaries, allowances, leave or pensions, the approval of the President of India or the Governor as the case may be required. It is apparent that the Chief Justice of India and the Chief Justice of the High Court have been placed at a higher level in regard to the framing of rules containing the conditions of service. It is true that the President of India cannot be compelled to grant approval to the rules framed by the Chief Justice of India relating to salaries, allowances, leave or pensions, but it is equally true that when such rules has been framed by a very high dignitary of the State it should be looked upon with respect and unless there is very good reason not to grant approval, the approval should always be granted. If the President of India is of the view that the approval cannot be granted he cannot straightway refuse to grant such approval but before doing so there' must be exchange of thoughts between the President of India and the Chief Justice of India. 

 In Gurumoorthy's case (AIR 1971 SC 1850) this Court took the view that the unequivocal purpose and obvious intention of the framers of the Constitution in enacting Article 229 is that in the matter of appointments of officers and servants of a High Court, it is the Chief justice or his nominee who is to be the supreme authority and there can be no interference by the Executive except to the limited extent that is provided in that Article. The same observation will apply to the rules framed by the Chief Justice of India under Article 146(2) of the Constitution. 

 On the other hand, the Chief Justice of India has to apply his mind when he frames the rules under Article 146(2) with the assistance of his officers. In such circumstances, it would not be unreasonable to hold that the delegation of the legislative function on the Chief Justice of India and also on the President of India relating to the officers and servants of the Supreme Court involve, by necessary implication, the application of mind. So not only that the Chief Justice of India has to apply his mind to the framing of rules but also the Government has to apply its mind to the question of approval of the Rules framed by the Chief Justice of India relating to salaries, allowances, leave or pensions. This condition should be fulfilled  and should appear to have been so fulfilled from the records of both the Government and the Chief Justice of India. The application of mind will include exchange of thoughts and views between the Government and the Chief Justice of India and it is highly desirable that there should be a consensus between the two. The rules framed by the Chief Justice of India should normally be accepted by the Government and the question of exchange of thoughts and views will arise only when the Government is not in a position to accept the rules relating to salaries allowances, leave or pensions." 

 34. Even if there be any disagreement with the decision of the Hon'ble Chief Justice regarding the terms and conditions of the service, pay scale of the officer and employees of the Supreme Court, the Hon'ble President or the government ought to have exchange thought and view if any disagreement with the Hon'ble Chief Justice. Executive of government like Deputy Secretary is not authorized nor have any power to turn down the decision of the Hon'ble Chief Justice. The Hon'ble Chief Justice is not a person but an Institution of a country and protect the judiciary from the arbitrary and illegal action of the executive. The Hon'ble Chief Justice is to frame Rules with the assistance of his own Justices and officers of the Supreme Court to deferent function, allocation of status of staff and officers of the Supreme Court. Constitution created the separate entity apart from other services. The job of the officers and staffs of the Supreme Court highly technical and mental standing who are entitle to get special pay structure for their supremacy of the work field, work load, skill, responsibility, respectability undertaken by the employees and duties of various categories. 

 38. The impugned Memo No. অম/অবি/(বাস্ত-৫) বিবিধ-৭/৯৬-২০০৯/৫৩ issued under the signature of the respondent No. 2 is declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and the respondents are directed to refix the pay scale of the petitioner Jamadars with the pay scale of the Drivers of this Court and the respondents are further directed to give effect of the decision of the learned Chief Justice according to observation made earlier (regarding Pay fixation, VIP allowance, over time and pay scale) within three months from the date of receipt of this order.
